extracted.intended_audience: citizens and policymakers considering the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative guidance and standards on structuring the executive's treaty-making and appointment powers and the basic objects for constituting a federal judiciary; explains why particular allocations of power (President + Senate, two-thirds present, nomination with Senate consent, etc.) best balance energy and safety. Written to persuade voters and legislators about constitutional design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: President with Senate advice and consent to make treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This union is defended as combining the Executive's fitness for foreign negotiation with legislative participation to secure the public interest; it affords greater security than entrusting power solely to either the President or the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of treaties as distinct from ordinary legislative or executive acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties are 'CONTRACTS with foreign nations, which have the force of law, but derive it from the obligations of good faith. They are not rules prescribed by the sovereign to the subject, but agreements between sovereign and sovereign.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because treaties are sui generis, neither purely legislative nor purely executive, their making appropriately involves a mixed agency (Executive + part of legislature) rather than being assigned wholly to one branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against sole executive control of treaties (risks of entrusting an elective President alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting the entire power of making treaties to an elective magistrate of four years' duration would be 'utterly unsafe and improper' because such a man might be tempted to sacrifice duty to interest or ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History and human nature suggest an elective chief magistrate may be corruptible by foreign powers through avarice or ambition; therefore checks (Senate participation) are required to guard national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against Senate-alone treaty power (loss of Executive agency and foreign confidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: To entrust the power to the Senate alone would forfeit the advantages of the constitutional agency of the President; ministers appointed by the Senate alone would not enjoy the same confidence or weight with foreign powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate-only control could diminish the Union's effectiveness in external affairs and remove the additional security provided by Executive cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Representatives unsuitable for treaty-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The fluctuating and multitudinous composition of the House 'forbid us to expect' qualities essential for treaty trust: 'accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics; a steady and systematic adherence to the same views; ... decision, SECRECY, and despatch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, changeable bodies lack secrecy, decision, and expertise; their frequent calls and long sessions would produce inconvenience and expense in progressive stages of treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-thirds of senators PRESENT preferable to two-thirds of entire Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring two-thirds of members present avoids the tendency of larger fixed-proportion requirements to produce paralysis or near-unanimity when some members are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportion of attending members promotes punctuality and avoids making determinate attendance necessary; fixed proportions of the whole may, in practice, amount to unanimity and lead to 'impotence, perplexity, and disorder.'

rubrics_metrics.name: President nominates; Senate advises and consents for appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'is to NOMINATE, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint' principal officers; Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement combines the advantages of a single discerning nominator with the corrective restraint of a legislative body, promoting judicious choices while avoiding the evils of sole appointment power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single nominative judgment preferable for candidate assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: One man of discernment (the President) is 'better fitted to analyze and estimate the peculiar qualities adapted to particular offices' than a collective assembly, and his sole responsibility begets greater care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sole nomination reduces distractions from private attachments and factional bargaining that afflict collective appointing bodies; personal responsibility and reputation encourage impartial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's concurrence as an effective check on favoritism and source of stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of Senate concurrence is 'an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism' and 'would be an efficacious source of stability in the administration' since consent would be necessary to displace as well as to appoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The possibility of rejection motivates careful nomination; public observation of the Senate's role makes both Executive and Senate accountable for appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination captures benefits of appointment while avoiding its evils
rubrics_metrics.description: In the act of nomination the President's judgment alone is exercised; the power of nomination produces 'all the good of that of appointment, and would in a great measure avoid its evils.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no one can be appointed without prior nomination, the nomination power ensures the President's responsibility while the Senate's review prevents absolute executive appointment power and its attendant risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection by Senate unlikely to be used frivolously
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate will rarely overrule a President's nomination because they cannot assure a better candidate will be presented later and rejection would cast a stigma and reflect on the President's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate restraint is expected; refusals should occur only for 'special and strong reasons,' making the check strong but not obstructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against small private councils or 'councils of appointment' (evils of cabal and secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small secretive councils (as in some State constitutions) become 'conclaves' prone to cabal, intrigue, barter of votes, lack of public responsibility, and oligarchic tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bodies are more easily managed, operate out of public view, produce improper appointments, and eliminate clear accountability that a public Senate-approval process provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against vesting appointment power in the House of Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniting the House with appointment power is rejected because that body is 'so fluctuating and at the same time so numerous' that it is unfit; its size and variability would defeat stability and cause delays and embarrassments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The increasing potential size of the House would make it impractical and would undermine the stability that appointment-by-Senate seeks to preserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive's residual functional powers (informing, recommending, convening, receiving, executing, commissioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other executive powers include giving information to Congress of the state of the Union; recommending measures; convening either house on extraordinary occasions; adjourning them when they cannot agree; receiving ambassadors; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as necessary and unobjectionable authorities that complete the executive's energy while remaining compatible with republican safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointment power (filling vacancies during Senate recess)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'shall have power to fill up ALL VACANCIES which may happen DURING THE RECESS OF THE SENATE, by granting commissions which shall EXPIRE at the end of their next session.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision enables temporary staffing when the Senate is not in session, but the commissions are limited in duration to the end of the Senate's next session to preserve Senate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects for constituting the federal judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of constituting the judiciary embraces: (1) the mode of appointing the judges, (2) the tenure by which they are to hold their places, and (3) the partition of the judiciary authority between different courts and their relations to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three aspects (appointment, tenure, jurisdictional partition) are presented as the central design questions for a federal judicature; earlier appointment discussion applies to judges as well.
